utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Patricia Sellers for the Prosecution. With me today is Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, co-counsel, and our case manager, Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And I would like to say good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to our friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with John Jones I appear on behalf of Naser Oric. And with us this morning is our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Let me start because it is already irking my eye. I don't like the whole set-up. There is too much distance separating the accused from his counsel. I know that there is some kind of security rule or procedure in force relating to the exchange of documents between counsel and the accused, and I know that the officers here have got strict instructions which I would never even think of interfering with because they are security based and issued. However, I want to make sure that there is a way in which the accused can communicate with his counsel without -- please, Mr. Oric. So -- I think it's in 2006 in the peak of technological court development, it's unheard of that the accused has to draw our attention that he needs to give a piece of paper to his counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I remember the instructions well, you're not allowed to be emissaries or ambassadors for -- I know I am correct. So sometimes when there is proximity it's done. One doesn't have to abandon his chair. So I -- let's proceed. But I need you, Madam Registrar, to look into this. Maybe if it's -- if it's just a light that he can switch on which will alert you to the fact that he has got some piece of paper. I don't know. But in these -- in these days, that should be easily -- easily solved. All right. That's number one. But it immediately struck me. I mean, I would find it very inconvenient for me as a Defence counsel to be so detached from the accused. That's number one. Number two, there were -- there have been some developments since the last time we met. One relates to the extension of the word limit for the purpose of the final briefs. I have decided that, and I asked my staff to communicate our decision beforehand to you so that you would not need to wait and labour with uncertainty. So there has been -- the limit has been extended, as per the order that I have signed. The other thing is the -- the Prosecution, due to some mistake, basically, in the filing of the written statements of three witnesses that I need not mention the name of, pursuant to Rule 92 bis, the filing included some material that had been redacted on previous occasions, and it was filed in a non-redacted form. I take it that there was an exchange -- there has been an exchange between you and that there is no problem -- if you confirm to me that there is no problem, then I can proceed with the filings later on this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there also has been two other issues that were brought up to our attention. One is a document that was filed by the Defence alleging a further eleventh hour sort of violation of Rule 68. I take it, at least from the information that I have, that you wanted to take advantage of this -- today's sitting to make oral submissions in addition to what is contained in the filing. Of course you're free to do so, but please try to limit your oral submissions to five minutes and then you will have either the right to respond to it in writing or orally or today, as you prefer. Who wishes -- would like to address this from your bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, I will be addressing this issue, and I certainly won't need to develop what's in the notification at any length. I think it speaks for itself. It's really taking, as Your Honour said, advantage of today's sitting for a clarification really from the Prosecution, because my submission is that an explanation is called for and -- but I'll come to that in due course. But I certainly would only be a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Yes, Ms. Sellers, if you wish to address -- I'm not forcing you to address this matter orally today because you do have a right to address it formally in writing, in which case the matter will be considered closed in the written form and then we will decide it accordingly, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're prepared to address the issue orally today. We would reserve our right that if subsequent written filing were necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As long as we have the adequate time limit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you can address it now if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, I thought the Defence wanted to raise the matter and then we would reply to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understood this would be in the -- later in the day. I can certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do it now and then we concentrate on the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, we did indeed file last Friday, I believe it was, 3rd of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- 2006 notification of a grievous violation of Rule 68. In summary, on the 1st of March, after the last witness had testified, we received this CD which contained 400 pages of documents, including tens of orders issued by Nurif Rizvanovic as the commander of the Drina Division in the whole region covered by the indictment, Bratunac, Srebrenica, Vlasenica, Zvornik, in which he's issuing orders, receiving reports and basically acting as an autonomous military commander in that area. We drew attention to the fact that in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief they allege that the accused, our client, exercised supreme military control over the soldiers in the municipalities of Vlasenica, Bratunac, Srebrenica, Zvornik, and that our client was the only person who had control over the soldiers in the area and that he took all decisions affecting the military. In light of that we say it's absolutely clear that this is exculpatory material because it detracts, significantly detracts from that theory of the Prosecution and that therefore this is Rule 68 material. Now, nothing, in our submission, is more dangerous to a fair trial and nothing more troubling on the part of the Prosecution than to have exculpatory material withheld. We submit that this material was clearly in the possession of the Prosecution and not just in the possession but in the actual knowledge of the Prosecution. And in our filing we explain why we say that, namely, that the annex to this material shows that material has been analysed, the ERN numbers are the same ERN numbers as exhibits which have been used in this case, and that therefore it's clear that what has happened is the Prosecution had these 400 documents and that they simply went through at some stage and decided to select one or two or three which they thought they could use in this case, and then simply put the rest aside for, I don't know, a year, two, or three years, and then at the very last day of the trial, after the very last witness, submitted this material. And that to us is -- and we use the word scandalous, because it's hard to imagine something more in breach of the right to a fair trial than for the Prosecution simply to sit on this material and then hand it over at the eleventh hour. The reason why we raise this today and why I say that an explanation is called for from the Prosecution is that, in my submission, there are five questions which the Prosecution needs to answer. Firstly, when did they get this material; secondly, where did they get this material from, what's the source; thirdly, do they say that this material is not exculpatory, notwithstanding the fact that, as I say, it goes completely against their thesis that the accused was the sole commander in the area; if they concede that it is exculpatory -- well, let me put that differently. If it is -- if they say it's not exculpatory, then what about those paragraphs in their pre-trial brief? Are they still standing by those submissions or are they retracting them; and if they concede that this material is exculpatory, then why was it disclosed on the 1st of March, 2006, rather than several years ago? As I say, Your Honour, in the filing we, to a certain extent, threw up our hands and said, well, there's nothing we can do with this material at this stage, and we simply reserve our rights on appeal. But since we are here, I think it would be useful for all of us to have an explanation from the Prosecution, particularly as this may -- or almost certainly will arise on any subsequent appeal. Thank you, Your Honour, unless I can assist you further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Yes, Ms. Sellers, or whoever is going to be addressing this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be addressing this matter, if you will just give me two seconds. Your Honours, the Prosecution does take the Defence allegation of Rule 68 violation extremely serious. And they've called it a grievous violation. They haven't asked the Trial Chamber to do anything, to make any ruling, to take any action. They intimate that they will carry their burden to the Appeals Chamber. Therefore, the Prosecution would like to answer those questions and make the following submission. Firstly, primarily, the Prosecution has not committed a violation of Rule 68 in regard to the documents that the Defence refers to as the Rizvanovic documents. The central allegation of the Defence is that the material shows that Commander Rizvanovic is the overall commander of Bratunac, of Vlasenica, Zvornik, and Srebrenica, and that Naser Oric, as a commander of the Srebrenica armed forces was but a subordinate in the chain of command, not the overall. This is what the documents, if one looked at them, would purport to say. The Prosecution's case has always been that Naser Oric was in the chain of command under the 2nd Corps that was based in Tuzla. If the Defence now agrees that the Rizvanovic documents confirm the Prosecution's case that Rizvanovic was one of the intermediate commanders of Naser Oric, not only is that not exculpatory; rather, it inculpates Naser Oric. The Defence have construed their Rule 68 allegation around, on the one hand, a geographical premise that goes back to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. If Your Honours would take the time to look at some of the documents that the Defence received, they will see that the construction begs the question of content and possibility of the answer having been misleading. Could we go back to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. I would ask you to look at Sanctions, Your Honour, and we can go back to paragraph 121 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. Your Honours might notice that the Defence has pulled out paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment because we are not getting Sanction. No, it should be this one but it says no connection -- it's come on now, come on now, yeah, okay. That's the one. But there was no connection until a second ago or two seconds ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. If Your Honours look at paragraph 121 that the Defence has pulled out, noting that Naser Oric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have a problem? One moment. Excuse me one moment. Yes, the -- yours is good. Is it okay now? All right. Okay. The problem was it was out of focus, blurred, and Judge Eser couldn't read it. So -- but it's legible now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you see that in paragraph 121 of the Prosecution pre-trial brief that: "Naser Oric was the only person who had control over the soldiers in the area. He took all decisions affecting the military." I believe that's the source that the Defence has quoted. If one would look at that paragraph in its entirety and particularly the footnotes that it indicates, we might receive a explanation of what is meant by the only person who had control of the soldiers in the area. One of the footnotes is reference to Prosecution Exhibit 109. That is the B/C/S of 109, Your Honour, now the English of 109, and if one looks in the first paragraph it says: "At the meeting of the Crisis Staff of Srebrenica TO on the 1st of July, 1992, three decisions were made for solving some of the problems in the current situation on the territory controlled by the Srebrenica TO forces." That is the area that paragraph 121 is referring to. Paragraph 121 starts with the date of July 2nd. If one would look just further down on the same document where we see in the last two paragraphs it talks about Hamed Salihovic, it's the only time that we see that the chief of communications will be involved with both the municipality of Srebrenica and Bratunac. So communications information from Srebrenica to Bratunac, there is no hint -- as a matter of fact, it's been the Defence case that Naser Oric did not have any control over other sessions, and it's been the Prosecutor's case that up until a certain time period Naser Oric controlled an area based upon that of the Srebrenica TO. Your Honours, the Defence then refers to paragraph 110 of our pre-trial brief. If we can go to paragraph 110, and we'll note the first sentence in paragraph 110. "The Prosecution alleges that Naser Oric exercised supreme military control over the soldiers in the municipalities of Vlasenica, Bratunac, and Srebrenica." Again, the central allegation of the Rule 68 violation. I would ask that Your Honours remember that paragraphs 24 through 27 place into context paragraph -- the first sentence of paragraph 110. Paragraphs 24 to 27 give a chronology, and it notes that: "In early November of 1992" -- I believe that would be -- "upon its creation in early November 1992, Naser Oric was appointed the commander of the joint armed forces of the sub-region. His command encompassed the geographical regions of several municipalities, namely, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, Zvornik, in Eastern Bosnia." That is the content of the first sentence in 110. Because we have been told that Rule 68 violations have occurred because the Prosecution always said that Naser Oric was always the supreme military commander of these areas, we really have to distrust the premise, but I would like to take the Trial Chamber to a couple of the documents that have been disclosed to the Defence in relationship to their supposed finding of Rule 68 material. One document that they hold up as a prime document has the ERN number that ends with 0211054. They've placed this on one of the top paragraphs of their motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, which paragraph number is this? There is no top paragraph as far as I'm aware. If we can have a number so we can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She said ERN 0211054.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but a paragraph number. It's very hard to follow otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Top --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe it's paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the initial ones, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's paragraph 7, if you would just give me one second. I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, where the last sentence says: "In terms of Mr. Rizvanovic, he communicated with the 2nd Corps in Tuzla in that capacity, that he issued orders to the accused, I imagine the reference to Naser Oric, thereby treating him as his subordinate." If we would go to the document they are citing to. It's a document that ends in ERN number 0054. We'll put that up on Sanctions for Your Honour. We're having problems with Sanctions. Can I ask your indulgence for one or two seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me confer with my case manager.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, until Sanctions comes back up, is there any way that we might be able to use the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, if you could assist the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would apologise to the extent that you see that there is some writing on the document, and that was writing that's work product, but we certainly don't mind sharing it with the Trial Chamber. This is the English translation of the document that's cited to in the first paragraph. This is where Naser Oric is being treated as a subordinate, and if you will notice that the document is a call for certain commanders to attend a meeting. And it's the commander of the Vlasenica Brigade, the Zvornik Brigade, commander of the municipal Territorial Defence staff, Naser Oric. And we see that companies and commanders from Urkovici, other places that we've heard testimony about, have been called. If we note that the date on this document is the 25th of September, hence Naser Oric being ordered, called to come to a meeting as a subordinate. And if we just move the document up a bit further we can see the signature on the document, Commander Nurif Rizvanovic. Well, first of all, Your Honour, we would like to note this calling of the military meeting that this document is talking about commanders, talking about Naser Oric as a commander. Certainly not exculpatory. It appears to me to be more inculpatory. I would now like to go to Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is document number -- exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: This is ERN -- it's not an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It's not -- yeah, but it was disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is part of the disclosure that the Defence is contesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make a note of it, can I ask you to repeat the ERN number, Ms. Sellers, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. The ERN number is 02110054. The Prosecution would like to show the Trial Chamber the contents of this document and thereby would like to see Prosecution Exhibit 137. That is in Sanctions, as I understand. We have it in English also. Now, if Your Honour would note, and it's a bit difficult to see, is that this is a letter now from Commander Rizvanovic to Naser Oric, commander of the Srebrenica armed forces, discussing, as a matter of fact, about the meeting. He says: "Congratulations on the magnificent success in liquidating Chetnik strongholds in Podravanje," which we remember in our evidence as around the 25th of September, "and sincere congratulations on your being recognised as the supreme commander of the armed forces." In regards to the meeting, if you look at his language: "It would be good if you came to the meeting. It would be best to resolve these issues in a joint meeting on Friday, the 2nd of October." It also talks about: "I'm expecting a shipment of weapons, medicines, and ammunition. It's up to you, commander, to decide if this is a priority." And then in addition, he talks about persons that he is sending them. He concludes by saying: "There area number of other issues that we need to resolve and this could be done if we discuss them and lay down common guidelines." Now, Your Honour, whether subordinate or a commander, this is a document that certainly is not exculpatory. Your Honour, we would just like to briefly continue on. Another document that was given to the Defence that they have mentioned in their notification - not motion - is document with ERN number 12110291 -- I'm sorry, it's 02110291. And it's a document which shows subordinate forces of the armed forces. And if we look in the document, we note -- Your Honour, we would have to just go a couple of pages. We're looking for the name Velid Sabic. Now, Velid Sabic is the commander of the 114th Brigade. The date on the document, Your Honours might note, September 9th. Defence is saying: Well, aha, proof, Velid Sabic was a subordinate to Mr. Rizvanovic, the Prosecution theory is flawed. Your Honour, we would like to remind the Trial Chamber again, yes, Velid Sabic was a commander, as we have alleged and some of the Defence witnesses have tried to deny. And we would like to take Your Honours to P80, one of the Prosecution exhibits, and in particular to the last page of P80. Your Honour, if you notice in the middle, we have the name Vejiz Sabic, brother of Velid Sabic. We've had testimony from Defence witnesses on that as to how they exchanged commands of the 114th Eastern Bosnian Brigade. And that was the date, beginning on November 1992, a sub-region was formed and then the Prosecution's case is that these men came under Naser Oric. The documents are compatible. The documents do not exonerate; the documents inculpate. We'd like to go now to the next set of documents where the Defence has said proof that Nurif Rizvanovic was the one who was in control. He was appointing people. He was appointing people captains, giving out ranks. One will notice in that series of documents that no one from Srebrenica was given a rank, but it's possible that there are other documents that exist where Nurif Rizvanovic gave members of the Srebrenica armed forces or TO ranks. We're not alleging that. We're saying: Let's look at some of the ranks that were handed out. I'd ask you to go to a document that has ERN number 02109958. In the English version, you'll notice that Nurija Fejzic was given a rank. It says that he was promoted to the rank of courier in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the rank of courier, very much in keeping with the Prosecution's case of the different functions that existed in brigades and commands. Now, the fact that Nurif Rizvanovic is making these appointments is also harmonious with the Prosecution's case in that we believe that that is what commanders do, and we've shown documents that that is exactly what Naser Oric has done within the Srebrenica armed forces. We'd like to go to the next document, Rule 68 document supposedly, ERN number 02110325, and here -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the one I'm seeing on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to go to the next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now I see the one that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document, as the Defence has told us, proof of command, proof of Nurif Rizvanovic's overall command because he is negotiating with the VRS as a commander. Well, let's look at these negotiations. Here the commander is talking to the VRS as a commander, supposedly Naser Oric's commander. Because this is Rule 68, if we look under subsection 2, what does a commander discuss? Corridors for humanitarian aid, observation of the principles of the Geneva Conventions. Very much in keeping with the Prosecution's case, if this was the superior -- if this were the superior of Naser Oric, then he had someone to talk to the Geneva Conventions about much earlier on. Your Honour, this document in no way is Rule 68 material. We would like to go to the next document ERN number 02110331 where the Defence has reminded us in paragraph 11 that Rizvanovic issues a great variety of orders on the 17th of October, 1992, to arrest Hamed Husic from Glogova. That's where he's from. Certainly can't tell by the document if that's where he is, whether he's stationed there, whether he's a soldier there, or maybe in Konjevic Polje. Let's look at that document. As a matter of fact, as a commander, he will imprison Mr. Husic for a period of ten years due to attempted rape of a minor person, and when normal conditions have been met for conducting the court proceedings, he will be brought before the people's court, that will possibly increase the sentence. Yes, acting as a commander; no, this is not a document that is exculpatory. Your Honour, if we could go to another document, and that will be document 02110278. Your Honour, one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do want to say that other documents have been presented, documents showing the setting up of a prison in Kamenica, that the Defence also talks about in paragraph 11, not set up by Nurif Rizvanovic but by a commander in Kamenica. The Prosecution certainly agrees, yes, you can set up prisons, you can punish people, you can detain people. As a matter of fact, that prison set up not just for crimes but for disturbances. That's another document they refer to where Semso Salihovic is mentioned. Again, we would refer the Trial Chamber to P80 showing when he came under Oric in the sub-region and another document that mentions a phenomenon called the intervention platoon. Intervention platoons were part of the different units and brigades of the ABiH. The document we have before us now is important because in this document it says that Srebrenica will send 200 men to partake in a battle. Is this an order from Nurif Rizvanovic ordering Naser Oric to send 200 men? If we go down the document and we look under number 7, Your Honour: "200 fighters for the same assignment and the same dead-line." Your Honour, this is an attack that within the document you see is to be around the 12th of October, the latest dead-line would be the 1st of November. If we go to the end of this document, let's see who signs the document. Commander of the armed forces Vlasenica, Kamenica, Bajrici, and Kalesija. There is no name of Nurif Rizvanovic signing the document. Possibly he asked or ordered someone else to do that. But, Your Honour, I would now ask you to look at some contents of this document, and for that could we go to document number 02110329 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I -- I have grave concerns about the way this is being presented, and certainly I'm going to have to respond at length to this. I understood that this was a question of -- of a brief submissions. The fact is there are 400 documents. If the Prosecution is going to go through 400 documents and explain how they interpret those documents, then we would have to go through the same exercise and point out all the.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- exculpatory ones -- The exercise is utterly futile, and it should be witnesses who talked about this and not Patricia Sellers telling us how she interprets these documents. That's the whole point. There are all sorts of ways to interpret these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you that this went beyond what I personally was expecting. I thought there was going to be a brief submission in responding to what had been pointed out or submitted by Mr. Jones and then we would look into the matter, but it has to turned out that it has not answered any of the questions that he put, except the one on whether you consider this material to be exculpatory or not and that you are going into great detail with the result that the whole idea, the whole exercise, that I had in mind for today would be defeated. In other words, I would still have to give the Defence the opportunity to respond in writing because obviously you -- I can't expect you to be prepared to respond orally to all this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's -- it's all also this point, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might respond prior to now Defence counsel responding, and since we've already discussed one issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest we stop here and you proceed with a proper filing and we take it up from there. He will have the opportunity to respond. Because this is not what I meant. I thought you would have a very simple explanation saying that you do not consider this to be exculpatory or you consider it to be exculpatory and come up with an explanation. I don't know. But certainly not to have a full-scale submission on each and every document explaining why you do not consider it to be exculpatory. I mean, if we need submissions on that, we will come back to you ourselves after we have seen what we will now ask you to file in writing. I think that's the only way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- yes. Your Honour, I have no problem with that. Might I just state one thing for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As we said in the very beginning, we take these allegations very seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very seriously. Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And that is the reason that we wanted to provide, even orally, a thorough answer. I have no intention of going through 400 documents. It seems to me that the Defence has assured itself that all of the 400 documents, from their analysis, not witness analysis, their analysis is Rule 68. It is only beholding on the Prosecutor to be as thorough in their response. What I would suggest, Your Honour, is that at this time point I have just very few other documents. We will not look at those, but we will submit in writing. I do not intend, neither, within our written submission, Your Honour, to go through 400 documents. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So by definition that whole process is not useful. If I might just make a couple of remarks generally in response to the submissions by Ms. Sellers this morning. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Mr. Jones, for cutting you like that. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Jones, finish what you have to say and then I'll give the floor to Ms. Sellers and close the argument there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well, Your Honour, what's also interesting about the submissions of Ms. Sellers is that she's been pointing to -- it's been a very selective presentation, first of all. It's only certain documents and it's certain parts of the documents which she's drawn your attention to. And the Prosecution is taking that position because in fact that really is the only position they can take that it's not Rule 68 otherwise it is such a clear and blatant violation that it would be a very serious matter. Now, Ms. Sellers said that our position is that our client was not a -- was in -- I had difficulty actually understanding her submission, but it was -- it was that we accepted that our client was in a chain of command and whether Nurif is above him in the chain of command or below him is a matter of insignificance, according to the Prosecution. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're following in the same mistake that you criticised Ms. Sellers for, because this again is -- I think should form part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Oh, I simply want to make our case clear. What I was going say, Your Honour, is that Your Honours are perfectly well aware of what our case is. Ms. Sellers's approach was to say: Oh, well, since in that document it refers to the accused as a Srebrenica commander, that fits in with our case, and therefore it's incriminating, it's not exculpatory, so no need to disclose it. Your Honour, just a few final remarks, if I may. Your Honours are also aware that the places in the indictment, Kravica, Jezestica, Fakovici, Bjelovac, are all in Bratunac municipality, they're not in Srebrenica, and do you know how much evidence has been given about Nurif's men coming into the area, their involvement in Jezestica in 1992, that Nurif's men are the only ones who had uniforms, or we had these 400 men with uniforms, and we have witnesses speaking about uniforms. Obviously an independent commander reporting to Tuzla, not under the accused's control is highly probative, highly relevant for our contention that any of these acts could have been committed by his men. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

The Defence did not show any or indicate any objection to this. I think from having gone through -- having gone through this document again and the part of the debate that we had last time, I think you still need to clarify, Ms. Sellers, which pages need -- really need to be replaced in P456, and which parts of the exhibits are redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now the discussion has moved from redacted page 8 and 9 to the proper redactions of page 6 and 7. So in essence we're talking about the proper redacted pages 6, 7, 8, 9, and with our addendum to the corrigendum, I believe that that matter should be resolved. And therefore after -- and if it is granted, we will hand up P456, having properly redacted pages 6, 7, 8, and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you have a position on that, Ms. Vidovic or Mr. Jones? You had not objected to the redaction of pages 8 and 9 basically so I don't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So please proceed along those lines as quickly as you can. P4 -- 561. I -- let me try to recapitulate because we are a little bit annoyed at this. You will recall that 561 corresponds to 458. We put the question to you -- or to Ms. -- to you anyway, I think it was you who answered this last time, whether you were relying on one or the other or both, and you indicated that the exhibit should be referred to as P561. The Defence in their document have, since the last meeting, have pointed out that the two are -- the two exhibits are different and have different ERN numbers. In addition, it was pointed out, and we can confirm it, that the first 30 pages that appear in P561 are missing from P458. So the Defence has suggested that in their opinion they cannot accept that these are one and the same document and that they have to consider these two documents as indeed two different exhibits. Question is whether you agree with this. Question -- next question is whether the fact that there are 30 pages in P561 that were not in P458 put P561 in more or less the same position as P598. This was not brought up by the Defence, this last issue, but of course it's in the back of my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the similarities in the situations. P561, if Your Honours recall, was the actual book in which what we refer to as the military log was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The 30 pages that are different are essentially blank pages. P458 entailed the photocopying of the pages that were not blank; therefore, it chose not to copy 30 blank pages and hence we have the difference. Now, if that makes the two documents different documents in terms of page number is correct, in terms of the substantive and relevant content for this Trial Chamber, I do not believe that there is a difference. Now, if we are to only refer to P458 in our submissions and not P561 for the substantive content, the Prosecution would be willing to concede. However, I do not believe that the fact that we have the two documents that are essentially the same that the issue as to the Prosecution trying to submit two different documents are not documents a la P598 should be taken into the serious consideration of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wouldn't agree that these pages are completely blank. On some of these 30 pages, you can see some annotations in handwriting. I've investigated that and I can claim that they are very important. And if we are ever in a position to have a witness who has drafted this document, it will be important. So I don't agree. Could you please look at the page number 03653736. That's why we insisted on these documents keeping their two exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we be practical. The Prosecution doesn't object to keeping both of them, the documents in. If someone wants to testify as to the first 30 pages, that's fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that will be the position. In other words, the two documents will remain in the record as P4 -- P458 and P561. You're both free to refer to either or both of them. Of course we wish -- at least I wish to make it clear that even a blank sheet of paper may turn up to be extremely important in criminal trials, as you all know, especially in this trial where we have got documents with loose papers and papers missing, sheets of paper missing, or obviously cut or removed. So the two will co-exist and you're free to make use of both, if necessary. P570. Now, you will recall that last time we met here I pointed out that the B/C/S version of this document is missing and needs to be provided by the OTP -- actually, I could have even referred you to previous transcripts where we had been given the impression that it was only a matter of the document being brought up or down on that same day. The B/C/S version was indeed tendered during the last sitting, on the 1st of March. Of course, the Defence has looked at it and has come back to us with some observations which are, for the record, the following. We are being told that the Prosecution disclosed what purported to be the B/C/S version of P570. According to the Defence, the B/C/S version contains many more pages than the English version. As an example, the B/C/S version bears the ERN 02115744 to 5781 as well as 5731, which has also been added. And it therefore has, according to the Prosecution -- according to the Defence, sorry, an additional 32 pages. The Defence does not accept that this B/C/S version is a version of real 5 -- P570. According to the Defence, the Prosecution should only tender the B/C/S pages that correspond to the English version that has been tendered into evidence already, namely, pages 5744 to 5781. According to the Defence, it is not permissible for the Prosecution to seek to tender 32 additional pages of additional documentation which have not been tendered in one of the working languages of the Tribunal previously in the course of these proceedings. Apart for this I just -- again for the record -- I'm not inviting any discussion on this. The Defence reiterates its objection to the authenticity of this document. Moreover, the Defence point out that there are some -- pointed out some errors in the English translations of pages 57 -- 7574 to -- 5 -- that's a mistake, 5774 to 5781 which emerge when these pages are compared with the B/C/S version. I don't need to go into details here. But it's certainly the case of calling upon you, Ms. Sellers, to come forward with some kind of position taken or clarification so that we will be in a better position to know how to deal with this now-tendered B/C/S version, which the Defence is contending is different from the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll get back to you with that, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And if it's much simpler to remove those 32 pages and address the mistakes in -- or sorry, the discrepancies in translation, I think it will be much helpful to the Trial Chamber. But of course, feel free to disagree with what I am suggesting. And if you need to have 32 additional pages, then of course we will need to address the matter more extensively because that would -- unless those 32 pages contain absolutely nothing, that would call for the discussion whether this is a new document or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understand you correctly, pages with nothing do contain something as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may contain something --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But we will look at them and we will certainly take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, may -- but while in the previous instance you will notice Ms. Vidovic did not stand up and tell you: Now you can do away with those first 30 pages; we don't need them. In this case, she is herself suggesting that you might think it more practical to remove those 31, 32 pages. So I'm taking her suggestion and putting it to you because there is, obviously, a difference between this and the previous one, as -- at least in my mind, if I am reading Ms. Vidovic and Mr. Jones correctly, but I think I am. So -- all right. So this is being treated differently by them, and that's why I'm making a different suggestion which I didn't make before. So you need to come back on -- to us on this, please. Yes, P600, P605, P607. You will recall that when we dealt with these documents, the Defence did, in a very succinct and laconic way, express an opinion there and then during the first March sitting. The Defence made it clear that they still objected to these exhibits and that in view of their objection we -- we had already basically taken the decision or we were taking the decision that rather than replacing, the new versions would co-exist with the original ones and we re-numbered -- we gave them a number. Now, there were some developments later on in due course in the wake of the Defence document. Now -- and I'll take these up one by one. On the 6th of March, the Defence explained the issue regarding P600 was solved in -- on the 29th of November, and we were reminded of the transcript of what went on on that day. I'm reported to have said: "So my record entry is not correct; it contains two pages in B/C/S and not one page." And Ms. Richardson said: "Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. And in fact, if we could have the usher's assistance in giving this document back to the witness so that he can see the second page. If there is no page, then I will provide it to you." I said: "Please provide it later. Let's not waste time. So he can read from my copy and we'll provide a full set." So on P600 now, do you still maintain that the two should co-exist or should P600.1 now sufficiently replace P600?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it can replace it. My understanding is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the way I understand it, too, but as --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I say, I have already sort of taken a decision - inviting my two colleagues to agree - that we would have 600 and 600.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because the witness saw that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's the position. We are making ourselves clear, hoping that everyone is understanding what is happening. All right. P605. Now, P605 is somewhat different, and the Defence maintains its objection. So the decision will be that P605.1 will continue to co-exist with P605 and detain -- the two exhibits will continue to be in the record. Basically, to explain, the Defence position, according to their submissions of the 6th of March -- I can state the following. This is basically an excerpt from the book monograph Golden Lily, et cetera. P605 as tendered originally consists of only two pages, ERN 5949, 5951. These two pages were shown to Defence Witness Mustafic on certain day. The Prosecution subsequently sought to tender additional pages from this book, namely, 5954 to 61 and 6125, and their respective translations thereof into English. 6125 contains information about Mirsad Karamujic. Mirsad Mustafic was asked questions by the Prosecution in cross-examination about this person, yet he did not have this page in front of him. If he had done, he would have been able to comment on the information contained therein, throwing light on its accuracy or inaccuracy. I mean, this is the Defence position; of course I'm not saying anything on behalf of the Trial Chamber. So the Defence points out that as a result, since 6125 was not shown to that witness and he did not comment or have the opportunity to comment upon it, they therefore object to the tendering of the additional pages from this book, namely, 5954 and 6125, as they were not shown to any witness and witnesses were, therefore, deprived of the opportunity of commenting upon them. So the position, briefly put is: 605, 605.1 will continue to co-exist; however, we will ultimately have to decide whether to allow 605.1 to be admitted or whether we will just throw it overboard in -- for the purposes of our final deliberations. All right. 607. 607, basically the position now taken by the Defence is that they do not really object to this document to the -- sorry, that the Defence continued to object to this document but not to the new translation. The position is as follows. This exhibit purports to be a list of the members of the Potocari Territorial Defence, GI -- Srebrenica, ERN 9572 to 9572, it's the same. The Defence objects to the authenticity of this document. The Defence agrees, however, to the Prosecution tendering a complete translation of P607, as the initial translation was only a translation of the headings of the document and was thus incomplete. So this will leave us with this position. There will be two 607s, one 607, one 607.1 with, of course, the open, unended question to be resolved as to the admissibility based on the Defence objection. That will remain unprejudiced and will be decided by us in due course. However, you need to address this question of the translation. We are not going to tell you what to do because this ultimately -- it is a little bit of an anomaly to an extent, but please let us know what you intend doing as regards the translation, since the Defence is indicating that they would not be opposing for a complete translation of that. If you don't agree or have some other ideas, please let us know and also inform the Defence accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that we could reach an agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So coming to the end now. Defence exhibit 690, Ms. Vidovic, Mr. Jones. The Defence have clarified their position on the 6th of March, for which I thank Madam Vidovic. According to the Defence, basically without my need to go into details, if the position they follow is that if there is no objection forthcoming from your part, the Defence would propose removing the other pages - I don't know -- I don't need to indicate them one by one - of this book as Exhibit 690, D690. In other words, you need to tell us if you object to the removal of the pages mentioned in the Defence document from the exhibit already tendered, and of course then we will need to decide accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that I'm going to consult with my colleagues in the very beginning of next week. The position right now as we would voice is that we would want the other pages to remain in, but if we can reach another decision, we will certainly convey it to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We would need to know because obviously we would need to take a decision, not necessarily need to -- this is the decision that we will be taking in the course of our deliberations, obviously. But if there is an agreement, it would help us immensely. Now, with D1014, D1019, and the corresponding point 1 in both cases, you will recall what I had stated on the 24th of January, 2006, to which I had drawn your attention. Same conditions apply to these two documents; therefore, I'm just reminding you about these original documents that are now part of the registry records, and I have got nothing to add. All right. That basically brings me to the end. There are -- yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, unless Your Honour has something else, I have two just very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I have got nothing else. That's why I say "this brings me to the end" of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Well, I just have very brief matter, and it will only take about 30 seconds I trust and it concerns closing arguments. And the issue is this: There's a remote possibility that we're considering that for certain issues of criminal law which are to be addressed or which we're going to make submissions about, that it might benefit to have someone outside our team to address certain of those submissions. There are certain concepts in criminal law, some of them, in fact, which are used in German law which are, in our submission, helpful and which I'm not confident that I will even be able to pronounce, let alone, expound upon. And so there's a possibility that we would consider having someone address the Trial Chamber on some legal issues, and I wanted just to see what the policy of -- was of the Trial Chamber, whether closing arguments would only be by counsel or whether, if we had let's say a professor who was going to address an issue, whether that might meet with your approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's put it like this: You've taken us by surprise. We are none -- I, for one, am not prepared now to deal with the matter without having further thorough consultation with my two counsel. It did occur to me once here in this Tribunal, and I can tell you that the Registrar had his own position on that and that the policy -- it's not just the policy of the Trial Chamber that you need to take into consideration, but also the policy of the Registrar and some practice directive relating to who could be in the courtroom and who couldn't. So of course we will be discussing this amongst yourselves [sic] but I would invite you to have a meeting with the Registrar or someone from his office. This is not the first time that the matter has come up, and I know that there is a solution. However, I will not pre-empt any issues now, particularly since I don't -- I don't quite know what the -- who you have in mind, what the Registrar's position in regard to that person could be, and whether -- and what would be the procedure that needs to be followed on your part before you present us with the request, et cetera. But I think you do understand and read between the lines that I think much of the parboiling and precooking has to be done elsewhere and not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we will look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It has happened to me before and I dealt with it, but also, of course, first thing is get the Registrar involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, we'll do that, Your Honour. And one very last matter is next week we're going to try and make courtesy copies available of our final brief before the weekend, because otherwise we might not -- parties might not have until the next Monday, not that we necessarily all want to work on a weekend, but that's the reality, given the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. And in fact, I mean I'm being extremely honest with you. I mean, what -- I know how hard-working both teams are, how dedicated to your tasks you both are, and this is why I publicly acknowledged now the work you did for the purpose of the aspect of authenticity of document. And it is unfortunate that at this last minutes when you should be concentrating your efforts on the pre-trial briefs and we should be still dealing with missing pages and this and that, et cetera. Please try to have everything ready in a best manner possible. I'm sure you appreciate that and we will have your cooperation. But it is frustrating to us that while we are also preparing a lot of things and engaging our staff on a lot of work and dedicating many of our hours, times, together to start discussing a few things, that we have also got to bother about these matters. Yes, did you say -- did you wish to say anything, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for the record, since we had another obligation, and that was to submit the translations of D590, D605, and D655, I would just like to say that we have provided those translations. We have done it before the beginning of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly. I understand that if you are finished with D1014 and D1019 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- I believe the Prosecution has the obligation to return those to the evidence unit, and would also like to state along with the Defence we will try and submit a courtesy copy of the closing brief prior to the weekend so that both parties are put in a same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, because you realise that after that the three of us, we will have to go into cloister and then in conclave. So it will -- and we will have a lot of pages to read and as Milton said, "inwardly digest." So I thank you so much. Also, albeit belatedly, at -- today is the 10th and we were not sitting on the 8th, International Women's Day, and since a lot of women take part in this case, both lead counsels now are women, plus assistant and whatever, plus interpreters, et cetera, please accept our warm -- best wishes two days later. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.59 p.m.
